source_refs.note: Topic 24.3.3 with Quick Check 24.4, answered (PDF 124-126). The book labels the methyl orange product 'p-dimethylaminoazobenzene' and draws it with N triple bond N; the lesson names it methyl orange (-N=N-). The coupling mechanism and photographs are summarised. Answers need review.

blocks.text: Phenylamine gives two types of reaction: those of the benzene ring and those of the -NH2 group. The ring carbons are sp2 hybridised and the nitrogen is sp3 hybridised.

blocks.alt: Phenylamine drawn with a Kekule benzene ring joined to an N atom carrying a lone pair and two H atoms. Arrows from a line labelled sp2 hybridized point up to the ring carbons; an arrow from sp3 hybridized points up to the N.
blocks.caption: Hybridisation in phenylamine: sp2 ring carbons and the nitrogen atom (original drawing after the textbook's unnumbered figure on PDF page 124).

blocks.text: The amino group is ortho-para directing and makes the benzene ring very reactive, especially at these positions. Bromination of phenylamine is therefore faster than that of benzene, and both ortho positions and the para position are substituted in a single reaction, giving a white precipitate of 2,4,6-tribromophenylamine: C6H5NH2 + 3Br2 -> C6H2Br3NH2 + 3HBr.

blocks.alt: Phenylamine (ring with NH2) + 3Br2 gives 2,4,6-tribromophenylamine (white precipitate), a ring with NH2 at the top and Br at the two ortho positions and the para position, + 3HBr.
blocks.caption: Bromination of phenylamine to 2,4,6-tribromophenylamine (original drawing after the textbook's unnumbered figure on PDF page 125).

blocks.text: b) With nitrous acid: diazonium salts

Phenylamine, a primary amine, reacts with nitrous acid to form a diazonium salt; this is diazotisation. Compounds with the diazonium group, -N2+ (written -N+ triple bond N), are diazo compounds. Nitrous acid is made in situ from sodium nitrite and HCl, and the mixture is kept below 10 C with ice, because diazonium salts are unstable and decompose easily, giving off nitrogen, even at room temperature: C6H5NH2 + HNO2 + HCl -> C6H5N2+ Cl- + 2H2O (below 10 C). On warming with water the salt gives phenol: C6H5N2+ Cl- + H2O -> C6H5OH + N2 + HCl.

blocks.alt: Three lines: NaNO2 + HCl gives HNO2 + NaCl; phenylamine + HNO2 + HCl, less than 10 degrees C, gives phenyldiazonium chloride (ring-N(+) triple bond N Cl-) + 2H2O; phenyldiazonium chloride + H2O, Heat, gives phenol + N2 + HCl.
blocks.caption: Diazotisation of phenylamine and hydrolysis of phenyldiazonium chloride to phenol (original drawing after the textbook's unnumbered figure on PDF page 125).

blocks.text: Alkyl diazonium salts are highly unstable under all conditions and cannot be isolated, but aryl diazonium salts are fairly stable at low temperatures. The extra stability comes from the delocalisation of the positive charge over the aromatic ring. Benzenediazonium salts are important intermediates in making many organic compounds.

blocks.alt: A Kekule benzene ring joined to N(+) triple bond N, with the + on the nitrogen attached to the ring.
blocks.caption: Structure of benzene diazonium ion (original drawing after the textbook's unnumbered figure on PDF page 125).

blocks.text: Aryl diazonium salts react with strongly activated aromatic compounds such as phenols and amines; these are coupling reactions, and their products, containing an -N=N- bond, are azo compounds. The positively charged diazonium ion acts as an electrophile and substitutes into the ring of phenol at the para position. Coupling with phenol occurs in mild alkaline solution, and with aromatic amines in mild acid: C6H5N2+ Cl- + C6H5OH -> C6H5-N=N-C6H4OH + HCl (NaOH), giving 4-hydroxyazobenzene, an orange solid.

blocks.alt: Over two lines: benzenediazonium chloride (ring-N(+) triple bond N Cl-) + phenol (ring-OH), with NaOH over the arrow, gives p-hydroxyazobenzene (orange solid), ring-N=N-ring-OH.
blocks.caption: Coupling of benzenediazonium chloride with phenol (original drawing after the textbook's unnumbered figure on PDF page 126).

blocks.alt: Mechanism: Ph-N=N(+) + phenol (Kekule ring) with curly arrows from the O lone pair and the ring pi bonds to the terminal N; the intermediate Ph-N=N-C(H) ring with C=O(+)H and curly arrows from the C-H bond into the ring and from the C=O bond onto O; then, with loss of H+, p-hydroxyazobenzene (an azo compound).
blocks.caption: Mechanism of the coupling of the diazonium ion with phenol (original drawing after the textbook's unnumbered figure on PDF page 126).

items: Butter yellow: benzenediazonium chloride couples with N,N-dimethylphenylamine in ethanoic acid to give 4-dimethylaminoazobenzene. It was once used in food but is now forbidden because it can cause cancer.

blocks.alt: Over two lines: benzenediazonium chloride (Kekule ring) + N,N-dimethylphenylamine (ring-N(CH3)2), with CH3COOH over the arrow, gives p-dimethylaminoazo benzene (butter yellow), ring-N=N-ring-N(CH3)2, + HCl.
blocks.caption: Formation of butter yellow (original drawing after the textbook's unnumbered figure on PDF page 126).

items: Methyl orange, an acid-base indicator, is made from diazotised sulphanilic acid and N,N-dimethylphenylamine.

blocks.alt: Over two lines: NaO3S-ring-N(+) triple bond N Cl- (diazotised sulphanilic acid) + N,N-dimethylphenylamine, with CH3COOH over the arrow, gives methyl orange, NaO3S-ring-N=N-ring-N(CH3)2, + HCl.
blocks.caption: Formation of methyl orange (original drawing after the textbook's unnumbered figure on PDF page 126).

items: The azo group (Ar-N=N-Ar) is a chromophore: it is responsible for the intense colours of azo dyes, from yellow and orange to red, blue and green, depending on the other groups on the rings. Many food colours contain azo dyes.

blocks.text: How would you prepare an azo dye from phenylamine and 2-methylphenol? Give the steps, equations and conditions.
